newsitem.title: USA: House Democrat offers new endangered species plan.
newsitem.headline: House Democrat offers new endangered species plan.

text.p: A key House Democrat Wednesday offered a plan to revamp the law to protect endangered wildlife that focuses on restoring populations to healthy levels and giving property owners more assurances of their rights.

"Currently the Endangered Species Act puts species on hold and landowners in limbo. The law must allow species to recover from their protected status and thrive," California Representative George Miller, ranking Democrat on the House Resources Committee, said.
Miller said his bill has the backing of wildlife advocates and incorporates concerns of property rights advocates who say the current law strips landowners of rights to use their property.

The bill calls for full protection of essential habitat when a species is listed as endangered, broadens the bases on which to list species, and judges land development on whether it helps species recover, not just whether it moves species closer to extinction.

But Miller said his bill also would help landowners by streamlining the process to get permits to use land designated as habitat, offering tax incentives to protect habitat, and capping liability to encourage the private sector to help make the law work.

With the bill, landowners could post a performance bond to cover expected costs to protect species which would be released when the Fish and Wildlife Service determines that the habitat recovery plan had been implemented.
If unforeseen circumstances raise the costs, that would be covered from a public trust fund, under the bill.

House Resources Committee Republicans led by panel Chairman Don Young of Alaska and Richard Pombo of California last year pushed an Endangered Species Act reform bill that critics said tilted the balance too far in favour of property owners at the expense of wildlife. That bill never reached the House floor.
Democrats' competing plans to strengthen wildlife protections also fizzled against Republican opposition.
"The committee made a run at gutting it. It's clear that a simple assault is not going to work," Miller said at a briefing. He said that should give Republicans more incentive to work with his bill.
Miller said the Clinton administration was not participating in this stage of writing a bill, which lawmakers have been trying to develop for about three years.
He also said he did not know how his bill compared with drafts that the Senate Environment Committee is working with.
